"executive_summary": "The Nipah Virus (NiV) poses a severe global health threat with a case fatality rate exceeding 75% and no approved treatments, prompting the World Health Organization to list it as a priority disease requiring accelerated R&D. This study addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for reported NiV inhibitors by creating a crowdsourced, publicly accessible knowledgebase called NVIK. The authors curated data from over 800 literature sources, manually verifying entries to construct a structured database of 182 inhibitors, including 98 unique small molecules. A rigorous data quality check involved a separate team of curators to ensure accuracy, with errors marked and verified. The study employed a combined evidence approach to prioritize these compounds, evaluating them based on two main criteria: the robustness of the assays used to identify them and their physicochemical drug-likeness properties. The team computed more than 1800 descriptors for the inhibitors and compared them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries to identify scaffolds with favorable profiles. Toxicity was assessed using PAINS and DruLito filters, revealing that only a few compounds passed all stringent criteria. The analysis highlighted significant chemical diversity within the dataset, with clustering showing that many inhibitors are structurally unique. Notably, some inhibitors demonstrated potent activity with IC50/EC50 values as low as 0.47 nM. The platform, built on LAMP server technology, allows users to browse, search, and submit new inhibitors, facilitating community engagement. By integrating assay robustness with drug-likeness metrics, the study provides a prioritized list of candidates for further development, offering a centralized resource to accelerate the discovery of effective NiV therapeutics and potentially repurpose existing drugs for other viral outbreaks.",

summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari; Ayush Upadhyay; Kishan Kalia; Rakesh Kumar; Kanika Tuteja; Rani Paul; Eugenia Covernton; Tina Sharma; Vinod Scaria; Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.executive_summary: The Nipah Virus (NiV) poses a severe global health threat with a case fatality rate exceeding 75% and no approved treatments, prompting the World Health Organization to list it as a priority disease requiring accelerated R&D. This study addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for reported NiV inhibitors by creating a crowdsourced, publicly accessible knowledgebase called NVIK. The authors curated data from over 800 literature sources, manually verifying entries to construct a structured database of 182 inhibitors, including 98 unique small molecules. A rigorous data quality check involved a separate team of curators to ensure accuracy, with errors marked and verified. The study employed a combined evidence approach to prioritize these compounds, evaluating them based on two main criteria: the robustness of the assays used to identify them and their physicochemical drug-likeness properties. The team computed more than 1800 descriptors for the inhibitors and compared them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries to identify scaffolds with favorable profiles. Toxicity was assessed using PAINS and DruLito filters, revealing that only a few compounds passed all stringent criteria. The analysis highlighted significant chemical diversity within the dataset, with clustering showing that many inhibitors are structurally unique. Notably, some inhibitors demonstrated potent activity with IC50/EC50 values as low as 0.47 nM. The platform, built on LAMP server technology, allows users to browse, search, and submit new inhibitors, facilitating community engagement. By integrating assay robustness with drug-likeness metrics, the study provides a prioritized list of candidates for further development, offering a centralized resource to accelerate the discovery of effective NiV therapeutics and potentially repurpose existing drugs for other viral outbreaks.

claims.description: A combined evidence strategy effectively prioritizes Nipah Virus Inhibitors by integrating assay robustness and drug-likeness.
The NVIK database provides a chemically diverse set of inhibitors with varying potencies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The Nipah Virus (NiV) poses a severe global health threat with a case fatality rate exceeding 75% and no approved treatments, prompting the World Health Organization to list it as a priority disease requiring accelerated R&D. This study addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for reported NiV inhibitors by creating a crowdsourced, publicly accessible knowledgebase called NVIK. The authors curated data from over 800 literature sources, manually verifying entries to construct a structured database of 182 inhibitors, including 98 unique small molecules. A rigorous data quality check involved a separate team of curators to ensure accuracy, with errors marked and verified. The study employed a combined evidence approach to prioritize these compounds, evaluating them based on two main criteria: the robustness of the assays used to identify them and their physicochemical drug-likeness properties. The team computed more than 1800 descriptors for the inhibitors and compared them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries to identify scaffolds with favorable profiles. Toxicity was assessed using PAINS and DruLito filters, revealing that only a few compounds passed all stringent criteria. The analysis highlighted significant chemical diversity within the dataset, with clustering showing that many inhibitors are structurally unique. Notably, some inhibitors demonstrated potent activity with IC50/EC50 values as low as 0.47 nM. The platform, built on LAMP server technology, allows users to browse, search, and submit new inhibitors, facilitating community engagement. By integrating assay robustness with drug-likeness metrics, the study provides a prioritized list of candidates for further development, offering a centralized resource to accelerate the discovery of effective NiV therapeutics and potentially repurpose existing drugs for other viral outbreaks.

Research Context
Nipah virus causes severe disease and death in people with over 75% case fatality rate. Lack of treatment has forced the containment methods to be restricted to isolation and surveillance. WHO's 'R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases' (2018) indicates that there is an urgent need for accelerated research & development for addressing NiV. Despite reports of nipah virus inhibitors, no systematic evaluation of the reported compounds is performed. The ones with focus on Nipah virus inhibitors are either scattered datasets or curated versions with limited or no evaluation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a combined evidence approach effectively prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors? Will prioritization based on assay robustness and drug-likeness identify superior candidates? Do the curated inhibitors exhibit physicochemical properties similar to FDA approved drugs? Can a crowdsourced model successfully create a comprehensive knowledgebase of NVIs? Are there non-toxic, drug-like compounds among the reported inhibitors?

Methodological Details
PubMed and Google were the two main sources considered for collecting the inhibitors. Research papers relevant to the study were downloaded using the query as 'Nipah'. At the time of curation this keyword listed 838 papers which were considered for data-mining. Papers with score values of 10, 5 and 4 were considered for further study. Data curation and quality check was done manually and the data is stored in NVIK-Open resource Sheet. A separate team of curators re-performed the curation independent of the initial team. Errors are marked in 'Red' in the curation sheet and was then marked 'Green' once verified. Each entry was tagged with its contributor's email Id. The Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK) is developed using the open source LAMP server technology. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Near neighbours (NNs) in NVIK are identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0). The clusters of NVIs have been obtained using Jarp (version 6.0.2). A threshold of 0.15 is used as the dissimilarity coefficient. At present, NVIK has 182 entries. The focus of the study was to evaluate small molecule inhibitors which were 125 entries. Of these 125 entries, 98 are unique nipah inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values could be obtained for 70 compounds. The EC50/IC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for 182 entries. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters of which 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons. Comparison of NVIs is done with FDA approved compounds (2346) and antivirals obtained from Enamine library (4644). DruLito is used which screens all compounds based on eight filters. Only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than CMC filter.

Procedures And Architectures
The web-interface has provision for text, structure and complex query based search. A submission form has been provided that can be used to submit new compounds. The database also lists database statistics along with the physicochemical properties. Simple Search option is to retrieve information using a text-based query. NVIK's query builder option enables search using complex queries with logical operators. An extensive 'Structure Search' interface is also available in NVIK. The user can query using SMILES, SDF and MOL formats. Users can also draw a compound in JSME browser that may be searched. Data on NVIs can be browsed for physicochemical properties like molecular weight. The database can also be browsed from major fields as shown in Figure 1. Near neighbours (NNs) in NVIK are identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0). Clusters of NVIs have been obtained using Jarp (version 6.0.2). A threshold of 0.15 is used as the dissimilarity coefficient. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. We have customized a CIRCOS in one of our earlier studies. In customized CIRCOS, 98 inhibitors are defined with a band having a width of 1000. To view the the compounds clusters, a compound network diagram (CND) was made using Cytoscape. In order to prioritize NVIs for further studies, we performed an independent evaluation. Based on this analysis, we prioritised 11 NVIs. NVIC0025, NVIC0032 and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters. NVIC0048 displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibits better activity among the three.

Key Results
A wellcurated structured knowledgebase of 182 NVIs with 98 small molecule inhibitors was created. The reported IC50/EC50 values for some of these inhibitors are in the nanomolar range -as low as 0.47 nM. Of 98, a few compounds passed DruLito & PAINS filters exhibiting drug-like properties. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters of which 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons. For the majority of NVIs, the distribution of all the six properties is similar to FDA approved drugs. In total, there are 34 NVIs similar to 76 FDA approved drugs. Only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than CMC filter. Based on this analysis, we prioritised 11 NVIs. NVIC0025, NVIC0032 and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and were accepted in FAF drugs analysis. NVIC0048 displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibits better activity among the three and has considerable overlap. The EC50/IC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for 182 entries. The EC50/IC50 values range from 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM for 125 small molecule entries.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The highlight of the approach is that prioritization of NVIs was performed not only by evaluating their druglike properties but also based on the robustness of the assays. This illustrates that the NVIK library is chemically diverse. Therefore, this approach is useful in identifying potential pharmacophore features that are important in contributing to the antiviral properties. The platform may offer a centralized resource for the community to submit and access NVIs in a seamless manner. Not only for Nipah but these compounds may be utilized for their antiviral activity for other viruses too. The future of drug discovery of outbreak strains is in engaging wider scientific community in continous curation and analysis.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ones with focus on Nipah virus inhibitors are either scattered datasets or curated versions with limited or no evaluation. Only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than CMC filter. Broad-spectrum antiviral ribavirin has shown contradictory results with even the most optimistic ones significantly below 50% in causing reduction of the mortality rate. Errors are marked in 'Red' in the curation sheet and was then marked 'Green' once the data is verified by both the teams. The scope of the current study was to perform a systematic evaluation ... for proposing a list of prioritized candidates. Some of the earlier studies report nipah inhibitors based on screening of large libraries within BSL-4 settings.

Claims
A combined evidence strategy effectively prioritizes Nipah Virus Inhibitors by integrating assay robustness and drug-likeness. Based on this analysis, we prioritised 11 NVIs. NVIC0048 displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. Only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than CMC filter. The platform may offer a centralized resource for the community to submit and access NVIs.
The NVIK database provides a chemically diverse set of inhibitors with varying potencies. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters of which 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons. The reported IC50/EC50 values for some of these inhibitors are in the nanomolar range -as low as 0.47 nM. The EC50/IC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for 182 entries. This illustrates that the NVIK library is chemically diverse.

Data And Code Availability
The data curated from literature along with all these analyses is made available on a web-based platform. The data is stored in NVIK-Open resource Sheet which served as the crowdsourcing platform. The platform has the provision to submit new inhibitors as and when reported by the community.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
In order to prioritize NVIs for further studies, we performed an independent evaluation of the compounds based on the robustness of the assays. A separate team of curators re-performed the curation independent of the initial team. Errors are marked in 'Red' in the curation sheet and was then marked 'Green' once the data is verified by both the teams.
